rewritten_text:
The party separated and settled upon two neighbouring benches. Anne sat with those in front, and Mr Elliot, aided by his friend Colonel Wallis, had contrived so cleverly as to secure the place beside her. Miss Elliot, encircled by her cousins and receiving the greater share of Colonel Wallis’s attentions, was perfectly satisfied.

Anne was in the happiest possible frame of mind for the evening’s entertainment; it supplied precisely enough occupation. She had sensibility for the tender, liveliness for the cheerful, attention for the learned, and endurance for the tedious. Never had she enjoyed a concert more, at least throughout the first act. Near its conclusion, in the pause following an Italian song, she interpreted its words for Mr Elliot. A concert bill lay between them.

“This,” she said, “is something like the sense—or rather the meaning of the words, since one certainly cannot speak of sense in an Italian love-song. It is as close to their meaning as I can manage, for I claim no understanding of the language. My Italian scholarship is very poor.”

“Yes, indeed, I perceive that. Clearly you know nothing about it. You merely understand enough to translate at sight these inverted, rearranged, abbreviated Italian verses into lucid, intelligible, graceful English. There is no need to insist upon your ignorance. The proof is complete.”

“I will not resist such generous courtesy, but I should dread examination by anyone truly proficient.”

“I have not enjoyed visiting Camden Place for so long,” he answered, “without learning something of Miss Anne Elliot. I consider her too modest for the world to discover even half her accomplishments, and too accomplished for modesty to come naturally to any other woman.”

“For shame, for shame! Such excessive flattery. I have forgotten what comes next,” she said, turning towards the bill.

“Perhaps,” Mr Elliot replied quietly, “I have known your character longer than you suppose.”

“Really? How could that be? You can only have known it since my arrival in Bath, unless my family had spoken of me to you earlier.”

“I knew of you long before you came to Bath. People intimately acquainted with you had described you to me. Your character has been familiar to me for years: your appearance, temper, accomplishments, manners—all were present in my thoughts.”

Mr Elliot obtained exactly the interest he had hoped to awaken. No one can resist the attraction of a mystery like this.

The chain of events that always brought suffering would have had to break, and the cruel fate controlling it would not allow her eternal laws to be violated. But why should I complain? Misery was my natural element; only miserable things could come near me. Had Woodville been happy, I would never have known him. After years of feeding on tears and growing under the rain of sorrow, can I now hesitate to tell a story of grief and death?

Woodville had to travel into the country, where business delayed him day after day, keeping him painfully separated from his lovely bride. A letter arrived in which she said she was a little ill and begged him to hurry back. Looking into his eyes would restore her health, she wrote; his company would be her best medicine. He was detained another three days before he could rush to her. For reasons he could not explain, his heart predicted disaster. He had received no further letter and feared she was worse. This fear left him restless and desperate to see her standing before him again, beautiful and well. All the while, a sinister voice seemed to whisper, “You will never see her as she was again.”

When he reached her home, everything was silent. He passed through several rooms and found a servant in one, weeping bitterly. Weak with fear, he could barely ask, “Is she dead?” He only just heard the terrible answer: “Not yet.” Shocking as the words were, they seemed less dreadful than those he had expected. Knowing she still lived and he could still hope gave him some relief. Remembering her letter, he allowed himself the wild belief that his kisses, breathing warmth, life, and love into her, would renew her strength. She could not die with him beside her. His presence would protect her life.

He hurried into her sickroom. Her cheeks burned with fever, but her eyes were closed and she seemed unconscious. He gathered her in his arms and pressed breathless kisses against her burning lips. In a voice of restrained anguish, he called her by the tenderest names. “Come back, Elinor. I am here, your life, your love. Come back, dearest. You promised me this gift: that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit recover. You cannot die beside me. What is death? Never seeing you again? Losing a part of myself, without whom I have neither a past nor a future?

Dawn had arrived when I put down the manuscript. The rain had almost stopped; the world looked gray and sorrowful, and the spent storm sighed and sobbed its way to sleep. I went to the stranger’s room and listened outside his partly open door. Hearing his voice, I knocked. No answer came, though he kept speaking. I looked inside. He lay on his back, talking in broken but energetic phrases and emphasizing them with restless movements of his arms, thrashing as people do in a feverish delirium. I entered quietly and leaned over him. He continued muttering and exclaiming. I spoke a single word to get his attention. Instantly his glassy eyes and ashen face lit up with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome.

“Oh, Sandy, you’re finally here! How I’ve missed you! Sit beside me. Don’t go away. Never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where’s your hand? Give it to me, darling; let me hold it. There. Everything is all right now, everything is peaceful, and I’m happy again. We’re happy again, aren’t we, Sandy? You look so faint and indistinct, like mist or a cloud, but you’re here, and that is happiness enough. I have your hand. Don’t pull it away. It’s only for a little while; I won’t need it long.... Was that the child?... Hello-Central!... She doesn’t answer. Is she asleep? Bring her when she wakes so I can touch her hands, her face, her hair, and say goodbye.... Sandy! Yes, you’re still there. I drifted away for a moment and thought you had gone.... Have I been ill for long? I must have been. It feels like months. And the dreams! Such strange, terrible dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as life—delirium, of course, but so real! I thought the king had died. I thought you were in Gaul and couldn’t come home. I thought there was a revolution. In the wild madness of those dreams, Clarence and I, with a handful of my cadets, fought and wiped out every knight in England! And even that wasn’t the strangest part. I seemed to come from a distant age that hasn’t happened yet, centuries in the future. That felt as real as everything else! I seemed to fly backward from that age into ours, then forward again, and find myself stranded, a lonely stranger in that unfamiliar England. Thirteen centuries opened between you and me, between me and my home and friends, between me and everything I love, everything that could make life worth living!
